content:
Apple has submitted its proposal for the fees it would charge for transactions outside of its App Store system in the Epic Games case. Details below.

Apple submits App Store outside commission proposal

After multiple requests to halt district court proceedings, Apple has finally submitted its proposal, suggesting a fee structure. The district court hearing will determine how much, if anything, Apple can charge for transactions outside of its App Store IAP system.

Apple's timing for submitting its proposal comes right after the Supreme Court rejected Apple's request. Apple had originally hoped to halt the lower court hearing while the Supreme Court reviewed the case—which centres on whether Apple can be held in contempt—while it currently charges a 27% commission on transactions outside of the App Store. This stems from an injunction issued by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

Apple argued in the lower court, and subsequently before the Supreme Court, that the court's decision could affect the outcome of the fee-determination hearing, and therefore the hearing should be stayed until the court issued its ruling. However, the Supreme Court rejected Apple's request, allowing the lower court hearing to proceed while the review takes place.

Accordingly, here's what Apple has now submitted as its proposal:

Standard apps would be charged 15% (this category currently pays a 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission); Video Partner Program ("VPP"), News Partner Program ("NPP"), Mini Apps Partner Program ("MPP"), and subscription renewals would be charged 10%; apps under the Small Business Program would be charged 5%.

Apple stated that "the factual and expert evidence relating to these proposed commission rates has been submitted together." The company added:

Apple added that "the proposed outside-link commission can also be compared with the commissions of other competing app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also pointed out that "Google Play Store's outside-link fees are 20% standard, 15% for programs, and 10% for subscriptions — rates that Epic actually accepted at the time."

Apple stated that it still believes the fee-determination hearing should be halted while the case is before the Supreme Court, and added that this submission is only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also noted that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on outside-link purchase commissions, ruling that it only becomes a problem when the commission is actually deterred.

With the proposal now submitted, Epic will have the opportunity to respond, and Apple is expected to file its brief with the Supreme Court by September 14.
